EssayChina

AI’s Weakness Is That It Rarely Makes Mistakes

Yu Hua is not worried that AI might replace writers. Human beings found “truth” through countless mistakes, he says, while AI’s weakness is that it rarely makes any.

Yu Hua Novelist

Can AI Replace Writers

I am not particularly worried about AI replacing writers. The year before last, I saw a report in the American media predicting that AI would replace fifty occupations. Writers were somewhere in the middle, in the twenties. So I am not worried. Even if AI does replace us, I will have attended more than twenty memorial services before it is our turn. By then, I will know what to wear.

My view has not changed: I still cannot see AI replacing human beings. Even if I let my imagination run without limits, I cannot picture it. What AI agents will be like is still a matter of speculation. We will only know once they are here. For now, AI has no real insight into life. Of course, I cannot claim any great insight into AI, either.

Human Greatness Lies in Making Mistakes

What is the most remarkable thing about human beings? We are always making mistakes. AI’s greatest weakness is that it almost never makes them. It sometimes hallucinates, presenting plausible but false information as fact. But point out the error, and it corrects itself almost at once. Humanity did not get where it is today by immediately accepting correction. We kept debating and arguing, and we kept making mistakes. The truths we know have essentially all been discovered through error. Without making mistakes, it is hard to discover truth.

AI today has no real insight into life. Newton did. To AI, an apple falling from a tree is just an apple falling from a tree. Newton saw gravity. Human beings have that capacity. AI’s thinking remains confined to a program; human thought can reach beyond it. That is where technological advances and great discoveries come from. Think of Einstein and relativity, or Bohr and quantum theory. Their thinking was not confined to a program.

These days, many people are talking about Hong Wang’s work on the Kakeya conjecture, a long-standing problem in geometry and analysis. How many conjectures are there in mathematics? In the late 1970s, when I had just started working as a dentist, the Chinese writer Xu Chi wrote Goldbach’s Conjecture, about the brilliant mathematician Chen Jingrun. Of all those conjectures, how many have been proved? Only a handful. Mathematical conjectures lie outside the bounds of a program.

Let me say it again: the most remarkable thing about us is that we are always making mistakes. Where do those mistakes come from? We create, make mistakes in the process, and discover truth through those mistakes. That is how it works. AI, on the other hand, does not make mistakes. As long as it stays within programs devised by human beings, I do not find it frightening. But if it ever starts making mistake after mistake and ignoring human attempts to correct it, perhaps that is when we should start to be afraid.

AI Writing and the Illusion of Shared Ownership

Using AI to write literature is dangerous. Why? Because it is so easy to end up repeating someone else’s work. I believe AI should never be used for writing. Some of the sentences it offers may have been taken from other people’s work. You may think AI is helping you write, but it is actually showing you someone else’s work. Put those sentences into your own writing, and you are using another person’s words.

AI creates the illusion that the sentences it offers belong to everyone. They do not. It has simply turned private property into common property. When we use those sentences in our own writing, we too are violating someone else’s ownership rights. That is how it works. So AI should never be used for writing.

But AI can be an excellent assistant in daily life. Let me give you an example. I have to apply for a U.S. visa in November. They gave me a form to fill out, and I had to look up some of the information myself. The first part was easy: details about my parents, my family, and myself. The hardest part was listing every country I had visited in the past five years, complete with dates. There I was, going through my passport and trying to piece together my travels from memory. After half an hour, I still had not found everything. Then it struck me: why hadn’t I asked AI?

So I asked, “Tell me about the writer Yu Hua’s overseas travels in the past five years.” AI immediately produced a list. From there, I went through the events I had attended, from the first to the last, and looked up interviews I had given. I was able to work out which countries I had visited, when I had left, and when I had returned. Then I filled in the visa application.

If AI Wrote Yu Hua’s Fiction in Mo Yan’s Voice

The Paris Review first asked me for a piece in 2009, but I kept putting it off. Last year, when the magazine’s deputy editor visited Beijing, I suggested publishing an excerpt from my novel Lu Keming’s Secret Smile, and he agreed. After returning to New York, however, he emailed to say that the editors had discussed it and hoped I would write a new short story instead. So I wrote “Sleeper Bus” and sent it to them last November. AI appears at the beginning of the story. After it was published, they told me it was the first short story in the magazine’s history to feature AI.

When DeepSeek first came out, everyone was trying it. I played around with it for two evenings. I asked it to write poems based on Zhang Xiaogang’s artwork and sent them to him. He was astonished. Zhang then asked AI to write poems about my novels and sent them to me. I thought they were quite good. I also asked AI to write a poem about the poet Ouyang Jianghe and sent it to him. He replied, “Poems like this have no soul.” I think he was absolutely right.

During a conversation, the host heard me talking about asking AI to write poetry. He then gave it this prompt: “Write a modern poem in Mo Yan’s style, using material from Lu Keming’s Secret Smile.” This is what it produced.

The Curve of Gaomi Township

“The soil of Gaomi Township turned over at the corner of his mouth. From that curve grew a donkey, carrying three sacks of moonlight that had never been entered in the books. The accountant said the books balanced; the donkey said, ‘Whoa.’ He said, ‘All it takes is a smile.’ The sorghum grew redder and redder, red as abacus beads, rolling into someone’s pocket and becoming a handful of copper coins that could sprout. He went down to the river, laughing, and suddenly the water froze. Beneath the ice, thirty thousand names were learning to bray like donkeys. Their cries shook the heavens, until the rusty curve at the corner of his mouth fell to the ground with a clang.”

As soon as I heard it, I said, “That isn’t Mo Yan’s language. It isn’t his language at all. It has simply put together a few elements from his fiction.”

The more original you are, the better your chances of “survival” in the age of AI. Writing is not simply a matter of technique. Some things can only be written from firsthand experience of life, with all its emotions and details. AI cannot do that yet.

Yu Hua Chinese novelist, author of To Live and Chronicle of a Blood Merchant.

DialogueKorea · Japan

A Common Front on AI

In an exchange of questions and answers, Yoon Seong-hoon, chair of the AI Future Strategy Committee at the Korea Publishers Society, and Takuo Murase, secretary of the Intellectual Property Committee at the Japan Book Publishers Association, compare how their industries are confronting generative AI, and what they could do together.

Yoon Seong-hoon CEO, Clayhouse; Chair, AI Future Strategy Committee, KOPUS

Takuo Murase Attorney; Secretary, Intellectual Property Committee, JBPA

1. Greetings and Self-Introduction

(1) Could you first briefly introduce yourself, including your current role at your organization?

Murase: After graduating from university in 1985, I joined Shinchosha, where I worked in magazine editing, audiovisual and other publishing-related businesses, and digital publishing. While working there, I came to recognize the need for legal knowledge, took the bar examination, and passed. I registered as an attorney in 2006, and since then my work has centered on intellectual-property law related to publishing, audiovisual media, and related fields. My involvement in producing the animated film Grave of the Fireflies while at Shinchosha also led to my current role as a director of Studio Ghibli. At the Japan Book Publishers Association, I serve as Secretary of the Intellectual Property Committee and chair working groups covering copyright-law reform, drafting model publishing contracts, and responding to generative AI.

Yoon: After graduating from university in 2010, I joined the Trade Publishing Division of Woongjin Thinkbig and began my publishing career as a literary editor. I then served as a senior team leader in the Content Development Division of Dasan Books before founding Clayhouse in 2021, where I continue to serve as CEO. Since 2026, I have chaired the AI Future Strategy Committee of the Korea Publishers Society (KOPUS), organizing AI forums, commissioning AI research, and announcing principles for AI use.

(2) Do you have any personal memories or episodes from past exchanges between the Korean and Japanese publishing industries that have stayed with you?

Murase: I haven’t personally been involved in international exchange within the publishing industry, so I don’t have a particular episode to share. On a purely personal note, my niece is currently studying as an undergraduate at Sogang University in Korea, and I watch a fair number of Korean dramas myself, so I feel a real fondness for Korean content. I am particularly interested in the many recent dramas based on webtoons.

Yoon: I attended the Japan Booksellers’ Award ceremony in 2024 because Welcome to the Hyunam-dong Bookshop, which we published, had won first place in the translated fiction category, and its author, Hwang Bo-reum, was receiving the award. At the ceremony, I realized that it was much more than an awards ceremony: it was truly a celebration for Japanese booksellers and publishing professionals. Their love of books and enthusiasm came through so vividly that I came away feeling inspired and energized. The staff at Shueisha, the book’s Japanese publisher, also welcomed us with warmth and kindness, making it a wonderful experience. Another book I am proud of is Kim Suhyun’s essay collection I Decided to Live as Me, which has been read by around 600,000 people in Japan. We have also published several Japanese novels that I dearly love, including Riku Onda’s spring and Chocolate Cosmos.

2. Current Situation — The Issues Being Most Actively Discussed Today

What topic is currently being most actively discussed in your country’s publishing industry with respect to AI and publishing? Please also share the background or circumstances that brought this issue to the forefront.(Examples: unauthorized use of copyrighted works as AI training data; the copyright status of AI-generated content.)

Murase: AI use is spreading rapidly across many areas of publishing, and it appears that authors themselves are also increasingly using AI.

Against this backdrop, publishers seem to be focused on issues such as the following:

  1. How should publishers’ content be valued when it is used for AI training or other AI applications?

  2. How much transparency can be demanded from AI companies regarding their training data and use of copyrighted works?

  3. As AI becomes more widespread, how will the application of the law and industry practice be affected with respect to summarizing, quoting, and restructuring books and articles?

  4. How will the growth of AI use change the ways publishing content is consumed and purchased?

  5. How should publishing contracts address AI use by both authors and publishers?

  6. To what extent should authors or publishers be held responsible for content generated or edited by AI?

As I will explain in more detail later, our association is seeking the cooperation of employees working on the front lines at individual publishers and has formed several working groups to consider how to address these issues.

Yoon: I think the issues surrounding AI and publishing can be divided into three broad themes.

The first is establishing principles of transparency for AI-generated manuscripts. There has been a sharp increase in books based on manuscripts generated by AI without sufficient human verification or control—so-called “one-click” books—and in cases where that fact is not disclosed. Some publishers indiscriminately received legal-deposit compensation from the National Library of Korea for such books, which became a major issue in the publishing industry. Fortunately, prompt action by the publishing industry and the National Library of Korea helped bring the problem somewhat under control. Subsequently, a broad consensus emerged among authors and publishing professionals that, to protect readers’ trust in publications, manuscripts generated by AI should be clearly identified as such. This led to a commitment to establish and jointly uphold a voluntary labeling system for AI use.

The second is how to introduce AI into publishing workflows as a tool to improve productivity. Because it can be used in many ways throughout the publishing process, from editing to marketing, we are exploring how to use it effectively and ethically. Even large companies have yet to establish organization-wide manuals for AI use, and individual employees appear to be using AI according to their own judgment without clear standards.

The last is compensation for the use of publishing content in AI training. Some AI companies are currently seeking to train on Korean-language publishing content in fields such as academic research and medicine. However, compensation standards and principles have not been established, and smaller publishers have limited bargaining power. As a result, some are permitting their content to be used for training without receiving reasonable compensation. Publishing organizations need to work together to establish compensation standards and principles and strengthen their bargaining power.

Each of these three themes involves numerous issues, and the Korean publishing industry is working to address them in various ways.

3. Legal and Institutional Framework — Existing Law and Unaddressed Areas

To what extent do your country’s current copyright law and government/ministry guidelines address issues concerning AI and publishing? Conversely, where do you see gaps that current law and guidelines have not yet adequately addressed?

Murase: Article 30-4 of the Copyright Act, introduced in the 2018 amendment, allows works to be used without the copyright holder’s permission, under certain conditions, when the use is “not intended to enable a person to enjoy the thoughts or feelings expressed in the work.” In addition, Articles 47-4 and 47-5 of the same Act permit use without the copyright holder’s permission within certain limits in connection with computer-based information processing.

These amendments were made with generative AI also in mind, but the speed of its spread today seems to have exceeded expectations. In an era when anyone can create and express themselves, many people have come to see this as an issue that affects them personally, prompting a wide range of discussions. Against this backdrop, the Legal Subcommittee under the Copyright Subdivision of the Cultural Council released its “General Understanding on AI and Copyright in Japan” on March 15, 2024. This document distinguishes between the AI training stage and the generation/use stage, and lays out how existing copyright law should be applied to cases involving generative AI.

At the training stage, the key question is essentially whether the use falls within the “non-enjoyment use” category under Article 30-4 discussed above. For the generation/use stage, the document states that whether rights have been infringed should be judged, as under conventional copyright law, by whether the generated content relies on and is similar to a pre-existing work (the requirements of “reliance” and “similarity”). As discussed below, the assessment of “reliance” is likely to hinge significantly on how transparent generative AI systems are made to be.

On July 31, 2024, a further document, the “Checklist and Guidance on AI and Copyright,” was released. It organizes what each party—AI developers, AI service providers, AI users, and copyright holders—should check from their respective standpoints.

Collecting and reproducing copyrighted works as training data for AI development can, in principle, fall within the scope of Article 30-4. However, it is explained that if using a work as AI training data unreasonably prejudices the interests the copyright holder would otherwise have enjoyed, the proviso to Article 30-4 may mean that the article does not apply.

For publishers, for example, a problematic case would be one in which “an AI company obtains and uses, for free and in bulk, book data that a publisher otherwise offers for a fee as AI training data.”

At present, however, there is no case law on this point, and the scope of the proviso remains unclear.

From the standpoint of promoting AI use, the Act on Promotion of Research and Development, and Utilization of Artificial Intelligence-Related Technology (the “AI Act”) was enacted on May 28, 2025, and came into full effect on September 1.

This law is intended to promote AI research, development, and use at the government-wide level, while also institutionalizing responses to AI-related risks. Based on this Act, a Basic Plan for Artificial Intelligence was adopted by Cabinet decision on December 23, 2025.

In addition, the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications and the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry have jointly formulated “AI Guidelines for Business,” which set out key practical rules for companies using or developing AI. The most recent version of these guidelines was updated on March 31, 2026. These guidelines are not legally binding. They explain how companies should manage AI use, covering safety matters such as privacy and security, as well as fairness considerations such as transparency and accountability.

Further, the “Principle Code on the Protection of Intellectual Property Rights and Transparency for the Appropriate Use of Generative AI,” developed through deliberation by the Intellectual Property Strategy Headquarters, was formally adopted on August 25, 2026. This Code is also not legally binding. It follows a “comply-or-explain” approach: companies are expected either to follow the principles or explain why they do not.

It sets out the following three principles and calls on AI companies to cooperate:

Principle 1 — AI companies should disclose to general users and rights holders an overview of their measures for transparency and intellectual property protection.

Principle 2 — AI companies should respond, in the course of legal proceedings and preparations for them, to requests from parties alleging infringement for disclosure of information concerning URLs or similar identifiers where the works at issue are posted.

Principle 3 — Where content identical or similar to a generative AI output exists, AI companies should respond to requests from the user who created that output for disclosure of information concerning URLs or similar identifiers where the identical or similar content is posted.

Of these, Principle 1 involves “public disclosure,” while Principles 2 and 3 involve “responding to individual inquiries”—a two-tier structure.

This Principle Code aims to reconcile continued progress in generative AI technology with adequate protection of intellectual property rights, so as to create a safe and reassuring environment for both rights holders and users of generative AI. During the deliberation process, however, the business community criticized the conditions as overly strict, and how widely the Code will actually take hold remains a question for the future. It should also be noted that even generative AI companies based outside Japan fall within the scope of the Principle Code if they provide services directed at Japan, which raises its own questions about its effectiveness in practice.

Yoon: In Korea, the Framework Act on the Development of Artificial Intelligence and the Establishment of a Foundation for Trust, commonly known as the “AI Basic Act,” has been in effect since January 2026. It sets out basic rules for promoting the AI industry while ensuring safety and trustworthiness, with particular emphasis on transparency in relation to generative AI. Providers of products or services using generative AI are required to inform users that the products or services are AI-based and to label AI-generated outputs as such.

The Ministry of Science and ICT also issued Guidelines for Ensuring AI Transparency to coincide with the law’s implementation. These provide more specific explanations of how AI companies should notify users when offering products or services that use generative AI, and how they should label AI-generated outputs. Taken together, the law and guidelines make one principle fairly clear: users should at least be able to tell when an output has been generated by AI. However, ordinary trade book publishers are unlikely to qualify as AI companies as defined by the AI Basic Act, so publishers are not obliged to follow these transparency guidelines.

On copyright, the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism and the Korea Copyright Commission have issued guidance on several occasions. Most recently, in February 2026, they published a Guide to Fair Use under Copyright Law for Training Generative AI on Copyrighted Works. Unlike Japan, however, Korea still has no provision that directly restricts or permits AI training. Whether copyrighted works may be used to train AI is therefore assessed under the general fair-use provision in Article 35-5 of the current Copyright Act. This involves considering the purpose and character of the use, the type and intended use of the work, the proportion of the work used, and the effect on the original work’s current or potential market. Consequently, there is considerable room for interpretation in individual AI-training cases, and the legal position remains difficult to predict with sufficient certainty.

Under these circumstances, many gaps remain from the publishing industry’s perspective. The industry is discussing whether to ensure transparency in AI use voluntarily, even without a legal obligation, and, if so, how. While these voluntary efforts are being made to ensure transparency about AI-generated outputs, we believe that transparency about what AI has been trained on remains insufficient. In practice, it is difficult for publishers or authors to check whether their books have been used to train a particular AI system. Nor are there clear standards for how to communicate their refusal to allow their works to be used for training and ensure that refusal is respected.

The same applies to compensation. Deals to provide publishing content for AI training are gradually emerging in Korea, but there are still no common standards on appropriate compensation, the handling of authors’ and publishers’ rights, or how individual publishers should negotiate with giant AI companies. In particular, as a market develops in which companies pay to train on publishing content, an important issue will be how far fair use should extend when other companies collect the same kinds of content in bulk, free of charge, for training.

4. Association Response — Guidelines and Activities

KOPUS is currently conducting research on issues surrounding publishing in the age of AI. We also understand from a Yonhap News Agency report (March 30, 2026) that the Japan Book Publishers Association is preparing related guidelines. Could you introduce any measures or guidelines your association is preparing for its member companies? If these are still being formulated or considered, we would appreciate hearing about their current progress as well.

Murase: Our Intellectual Property Committee (chaired by Hisato Imura, President of Keiso Shobo) launched a Generative AI Working Group on March 30 of this year to begin examining these issues. I serve as chair of that working group.

The working group established three subcommittees, each of which examined its assigned theme.

Subcommittee 1 is working to add clauses addressing AI use to the model publishing contract that our association has long prepared and provided to members. Since a publishing contract is an agreement between the copyright holder and the publisher, this work covers foundational matters such as clarifying each party’s responsibility when either the author or the publisher uses AI, and rules for handling rights when an AI company makes secondary use of a published work. That said, because publication types and individual companies’ policies vary considerably, in practice each company customizes this template to fit its own circumstances.

Subcommittee 2 is developing the principles that should inform guidelines governing publishers’ and their employees’ use of generative AI in the production and editing of publications. Rather than drafting a guideline document or template itself, this subcommittee aims to clarify what considerations are necessary and what options exist when each company drafts its own guidelines—serving as a forum for discussion that helps each publisher craft guidelines suited to its own particular business.

Subcommittee 3 aims to produce a “contract checklist” identifying the minimum contractual points publishers should confirm—including from the standpoint of protecting authors’ rights—when providing publication data to AI developers. Each company should decide for itself whether to license its data—that is, permit its use—and on what terms, including payment. The subcommittee deliberately leaves those decisions to individual companies. It focuses only on the minimum contract terms publishers and authors need to check to protect their rights.

Each subcommittee has been meeting actively since April, and their respective outputs have now almost reached the final-draft stage. We may be able to publish them as early as October.

Yoon: KOPUS is conducting research and pursuing policy initiatives to respond to the AI era. In April, we held an emergency forum to begin discussions with publishing professionals about AI’s impact on the industry and how we should respond. Professor Park Jung-in of the AI DynaInfo Research Institute at Duksung Women’s University led the commissioned research, and its findings were presented at the end of September. The research also included an in-depth survey to reflect the voices of people working in publishing. Participation was more active than we had expected: a total of 188 publishers took part and answered each question with considerable care. This provided an opportunity to see how much interest publishing professionals have in AI issues. The research team drew on this extensive and detailed survey data, together with analysis of overseas cases and legal frameworks.

At the forum presenting the research findings, we also announced Principles for AI Use by Publishers and Authors for the Benefit of Readers, separately from the report. The aim was to establish standards that the publishing industry could put into practice immediately, ahead of institutional reform. The key points of the research report and the principles are as follows.

The research report distinguished between two broad questions: how to manage publications created using AI, and how to protect existing publications when they are used for AI training. It proposed several priorities: labeling publications according to the extent of AI involvement, adding AI-related clauses to standard publishing contracts, establishing a reservation of rights (opt-out) for AI training, and improving transparency about training data. It also proposed a database of rights information and a system for licensing content collectively, so publishers can negotiate together rather than relying on their limited individual bargaining power.

Of these proposals, the parts that the publishing industry can put into practice voluntarily and immediately were set out in concrete form as the Principles for AI Use by Publishers and Authors for the Benefit of Readers. The key principle is that readers should be able to understand what work was entrusted to AI and who makes the final decisions and takes responsibility, rather than simply whether AI was used.

The principles are particularly meaningful because they are not a declaration by KOPUS alone: several publishing organizations and authors’ organizations participated together. In addition to publishing organizations such as the Council of Humanities and Social Sciences Publishers and the Korean Picture Book Publishers Association, the Writers Association of Korea also joined as a co-signatory. We believed that principles for the AI era would be difficult to make effective if publishers established them alone, and that they should be developed together with authors as creators.

We divided AI use into three categories, based not on how much AI was used but on whether humans sufficiently controlled and verified its output. Works authored by humans, with AI used only in limited ways such as basic proofreading and copyediting, drafting outlines, or organizing a table of contents, are classified as “human-authored works.” Works incorporating AI-generated material but completed under sufficient human control and verification are “AI-assisted works.” Publications in which human control and verification of AI-generated content are absent or insufficient are “AI-generated publications.” For AI-assisted works and AI-generated publications, we recommended indicating the category in a place readily visible to readers, such as the copyright page. The labeling guidelines also call for the text, translation, cover, illustrations, and other components to be assessed separately, rather than assigning a single category to the entire book. For example, if a human wrote the text but only the cover was created with AI, the disclosure would concern the cover alone, indicating the use of AI and whether the result was verified.

At the same time, we made clear that humans retain final responsibility for a book even when AI is used. Authors should personally verify the accuracy of information provided by AI, while publishers should take primary responsibility for checking the extent of AI use in a manuscript and disclose it transparently to readers. The principles also include information-security standards, such as not entering nonpublic information, including unpublished manuscripts or proposals, into AI systems without the rights holder’s prior consent.

On AI training, we stated that the use of publications as training data should be conditional on rights holders’ consent and fair compensation. The principles also call on publishers to make efforts to indicate whether they permit or refuse AI training on their books, and to require separate permission and compensation when AI companies use books to provide summaries, explanations, or other services that could serve as substitutes for the original works in the market.

For reference, more in-depth research on AI training is being conducted separately under a commission from the Korean Publishers Association, while research on how to use AI in the publishing industry is being conducted under a commission from the Publication Industry Promotion Agency of Korea. There may be some overlap with KOPUS’s research, but the three organizations each emphasize different areas. We expect that, as their findings accumulate, the studies will complement one another in developing a more comprehensive approach to the principles the Korean publishing industry should establish and the steps it should take in the AI era.

5. Cases from the Field — Changes Publishers Are Experiencing

Could you share specific examples of changes, challenges, or difficulties that publishers have actually experienced as a result of AI’s introduction and spread?(Examples: copyright disputes with overseas AI companies; introducing AI into translation and editing; adding AI-related clauses to contracts.)

Murase: With a few exceptions, Japanese publishers are small or medium-sized enterprises operating on a small scale with limited capital. As with efforts to combat digital piracy, these publishers face severe shortages of staff and funding, making it extremely difficult for any individual publisher to respond fully to generative AI on its own. The measures described in our answer to Question 4 are intended to support individual publishers, even if only to a limited degree. At the level of individual editors and writers, generative AI use will likely continue to spread; sharing the experience gained by individuals within their companies and across the industry is likely to become an important challenge.

Yoon: I understand that these problems are common across countries, and in Korea we are also seeing a sharp increase in manuscript submissions and entries to writing competitions. It is not difficult to infer that generative AI is the cause. Discovering promising new authors is becoming increasingly important, yet, paradoxically, it is also becoming increasingly difficult. In translated books, there have even been cases where people use AI to translate a work and then pay to use a translator’s name, misleading readers into thinking that a human translated the book. There is considerable concern that advances in AI technology may lead to even greater confusion. AI training has become a major issue among specialist academic publishers. (It has not yet become a direct concern for general trade publishers, but that seems to be only a matter of time.) We need to establish standards that allow publishers to receive fair compensation. There are also calls for effective training to prevent an AI divide between large and small companies, or between younger and older employees.

6. Outlook and Cooperation — The Next One to Two Years, and Korea-Japan/Asian Cooperation

How do you expect this issue to develop over the next one to two years? What opportunities do you see for the publishing industries of Korea, Japan, and Asia more broadly to work together on this challenge?

Murase: The spread of generative AI use is likely to bring major change to how publishing content is produced and edited. Gains in efficiency are a welcome development, but the tasks that generative AI takes over often overlap with work through which younger staff traditionally gained experience. This raises the risk that opportunities for developing new talent could disappear.

As noted in our answer to Question 5, publishers also tend to be relatively small in scale, making it difficult for individual editors or authors to stand up on their own against the giant companies that develop generative AI. Many useful generative AI systems will likely continue to be developed primarily in the United States and China going forward. Europe appears to face similar circumstances in some respects, but in Europe, efforts to exert some control over global AI companies continue through EU-level rules on personal data protection and generative AI. It would likely be difficult to bring a framework like the EU’s to the East Asian region, including Japan and Korea, but I hope our two countries can build enough combined influence to have at least some impact on the shaping of international rules.

Yoon: I do not know whether it would be possible, but I have imagined some bold possibilities. What if, when global AI companies request permission to train on publications from Korea and Japan, our two publishing industries joined forces and spoke with one voice to maximize our bargaining power? What if Korean and Japanese publishing professionals jointly announced an AI-labeling system to uphold principles of transparency and committed to following it together? If, amid the worldwide confusion caused by AI-generated publications, our two industries took the initiative to establish standards that could serve as a model not only for other Asian countries but for publishing industries around the world, that would be something to be very proud of. Even without such ambitious projects, communicating regularly, sharing the difficulties we face in practice, and exchanging our respective insights could help us respond more quickly and effectively to the many problems that arise.

7. Closing Remarks

Taking this dialogue as an opportunity, is there a final message you would like to convey to the publishing industries of both countries?

Murase: Compared to television or newspapers, publishing is a medium that can sustain itself with a relatively small readership. As a result, publishers and authors tend to compete by emphasizing what sets them apart from other publishers and authors. But the challenges posed by generative AI concern every stakeholder alike, and I believe it is important to recognize what we have in common and move forward together. Viewed from the perspective of publishing as a medium, individual differences are, in a sense, “minor differences,” and what is needed is an approach that keeps the larger shared cause in view. Even so, the Japanese publishing industry, at least, has tended to cling to those minor differences, sometimes in ways that risk losing sight of the bigger shared cause altogether. That may have been acceptable in an analog world, but I don’t think it will work the same way in a digital one. I believe we need a deliberate effort to change that mindset.

Yoon: The widespread adoption of smartphones has significantly reduced adult reading rates. The size of Korea’s publishing market has barely changed in nominal terms over thirty years, a shocking result when inflation and GDP growth are taken into account. I cannot be certain that the calculation is precise, but I think it is reasonable to consider the market to have effectively contracted by at least 50 percent. With the arrival of AI, however, the proportion of people who do not read books seems to be growing even faster. There are no precise statistics yet, but that is certainly how it feels in practice. The loss of readers appears particularly serious for nonfiction publications dealing with knowledge and information. Meanwhile, people in education report that students increasingly take AI use for granted and that their thinking and learning abilities have declined significantly. The publishing industries of Korea and Japan must make a strong case for reading as a way to address this problem. If we cannot prevent AI use, we need to persuade people to read books rather than watch videos as a counterbalance. We should work together toward a government announcement ambitious enough to declare an “era of reading,” and place even greater emphasis on the importance of reading education in schools. This is about more than the publishing industry’s survival: it has a profound impact on people’s abilities. I believe that the publishing industries of Korea and Japan must act with a strong sense of mission to communicate the importance of reading to the public and to our governments.

About the Contributors

Yoon Seong-hoon CEO of Clayhouse and chair of the AI Future Strategy Committee of the Korea Publishers Society (KOPUS).

Takuo Murase Attorney; secretary of the Intellectual Property Committee and chair of the Generative AI Working Group at the Japan Book Publishers Association (JBPA).

RoundtableKorea · Malaysia · Indonesia

Small Presses, New Tools

Independent publishers from Seoul, Kuala Lumpur and Jakarta share their hands-on experience with AI and talk about what makes publishing irreplaceable.

Sungil Noh Graphic designer and publisher, Sojanggak

Lew Kong Hui Founder and editor, Process Magazine

Wanda Kamarga Creative director, The 1984

Online, October 2, 2026

Sungil Noh

What kind of shifts are taking place in the Southeast Asian publishing industry in the era of AI? Over the past few years, through active exchanges—including publishing projects, collaborations, interviews, and events—with Southeast Asian creators, I’ve felt a wave of dynamic changes sweeping through the region’s publishing scene. Today, we are joined by two guests who are actively engaging with diverse creators and producing content at the heart of the publishing and art scenes in Indonesia and Malaysia.

Thank you for joining today’s interview about AI. Did you look over the questionnaires? How was it?

Kong Hui

It’s good. There are a lot of really interesting questions. Some of them hadn’t crossed my mind before, so it was good to have the questions challenge my thinking about this topic a little bit.

Sungil Noh

Nice. How about you, Wanda?

Wanda Kamarga

Likewise. These are things that have been on our minds over the past year—how we should all adapt. From the questionnaires, we do have experiences with almost all of those, so I’m ready. Thanks for inviting me.

Sungil Noh

Thank you so much. For this interview, I will ask questions based on the questionnaires step by step, and you can freely answer them. You can also jump in on each other’s answers anytime, so please feel free to talk about your experience and your thoughts.

Okay, then let’s start.

Local Content & Unique Linguistic Ecosystems

Sungil Noh

Let’s start with the first question. Could you tell us about the unique characteristics of languages, scripts, and local content in your country’s publishing market?

Kong Hui

Malaysia is a very multicultural country. We have English-speaking, Chinese-speaking, and Malay-speaking media, along with Tamil and so on. So as publishers, when we make a decision to publish something, it’s not simply a matter of translating it into another language. We have to consider the nuances that are so important to how a language is conveyed editorially and tonally. We need to ensure that whatever we originally created in English is properly made into a faithful version in other languages.

Wanda Kamarga

For Indonesia, we are an archipelago and very diverse, like Malaysia, with maybe hundreds of local languages. But as you may know, we have one main language, Bahasa Indonesia, which is compulsory for everyone. Everyone speaks Bahasa Indonesia, so most media is written in it.

As you try to learn Bahasa Indonesia, you might notice that the language in textbooks and the language people speak daily are very different. Our daily language is heavily nuanced with a lot of slang. In our literature, people often try to incorporate these nuances, because using too strict of a textbook Bahasa Indonesia doesn’t really represent people’s real stories or daily lives.

This is quite a unique trait in Indonesia. Maybe Malaysians are also familiar with this since our languages are somewhat similar, right? But in daily life, Indonesians use so much slang and take advantage of it to add more nuance to whatever context we’re trying to deliver. So if you ask about unique traits, that is definitely one. Sometimes we even throw regional languages in there.

Sungil Noh

Yeah, I feel both of you share a similar situation and environment in your publishing markets with language diversity. So let me follow up: With global AI tools like ChatGPT, do you feel limitations or a sense of Westernization?

Kong Hui

Well, I think definitely. Based on my experience, translation to Bahasa Malaysia is quite tricky for many popular Western models. We experimented with AI-assisted translation once or twice, but we felt that the output just didn’t feel right. To a non-native speaker, it might seem like it’s doing a good job, but anyone who speaks the language daily can tell that something is off. Editorial translation isn’t just about changing text into another language—as Wanda mentioned, capturing tone and how real people speak has to translate well, too. So we’ve never seriously considered creating content in another language purely through AI. 

Sungil Noh

Very interesting. How is it in the Indonesian context?

Wanda Kamarga

I don’t know how much data people are feeding into AI, but somehow these AIs kind of understand our nuances. If you enter something into ChatGPT and ask it to use “Jakarta slang” or “Balinese slang,” for example, it somehow understands that. But just as Kong Hui mentioned, yes, it does that, but the feeling isn’t there. It’s like it picks up these nuances from here and there, but it cannot recreate them in a truly natural way. I’ve noticed that the way Indonesian people speak day to day is very spontaneous and impromptu, which is something AI just cannot replicate. To be honest with you, AI understands it and picks it up very fast, but it just can’t recreate it.

Kong Hui

Yeah, agreed. I think it’s just the feeling that once you read it back, something seems off. But then again, it doesn’t need to be other languages. Even right now, if you look at just English, sometimes when you ask it to write something or the way it communicates to you, you get that sense that it’s not very natural, that it’s not how someone real would speak. That really throws us and other people off.

Sungil Noh

Me too. When I use AI tools in Korean, I feel like they understand Korean context and nuance very easily, so sometimes I’m really surprised. But what they still cannot understand are things like tradition and very sensitive issues. That said, technology has advanced these days and has become so easy to use.

Kong Hui

Definitely.

Sungil Noh

Thank you so much. Okay, then let’s go to the next question: is AI helping as a remote assistant, like bridging language gaps or sharing visual ideas between authors and designers?

Kong Hui

For us, we’re quite lucky because we work mostly with local designers and writers, so we haven’t really had that experience just yet. But if you want to talk about AI as an admin assistant, I think that’s where AI really comes in and helps a lot, because ultimately it’s a tool.

For us, AI really helps to transcribe some of these conversations with the people we work with, and that makes things a lot smoother. It saves time with the creation of recaps and meeting notes and it makes it super easy to go back and revisit past projects. So as a tool, AI has helped in that sense.

Sungil Noh

Yeah, I think Indonesia and Malaysia have geographical separation, right? So a remote assistant must be very important for you guys. It’s very interesting for me to see your context. Because Korea is socially monolingual and geographically like an island, I was curious about the context in other Southeast Asian countries.

How about you, Wanda?

Wanda Kamarga

In the context of regional languages, we don’t really rely on AI because, as I mentioned, everyone speaks Bahasa Indonesia. So between islands and regions, language is very easy. When you want to communicate a concept, you speak Bahasa Indonesia. You’re educated and trained so that in a professional setting, the default is Bahasa Indonesia—or most of the time right now, English. It’s kind of similar to our situation right now. In that way, we aren’t too reliant on AI.

When it comes to clarifying visual concepts, we are also very non-verbal and spontaneous people, so direct meetings, sending sketches, or sharing photos are often more helpful. But AI is more useful when we do menial tasks—tasks that require a lot of time, like processing data, generating ideas, and things like that.

Opportunities in AI: Translation, Publishing, and Regional Reach

Sungil Noh

Until now, I think we have rarely relied on AI tools in our daily lives. But for me, when working with foreigners, it’s really helpful for translation and communication. So I think this connects to the next question: Do you feel there are now bigger opportunities for local books to reach readers across Asia or the world?

Kong Hui

Well, we’ve had two types of experiences with this. A couple of years ago, we wanted to release a special magazine that was in two languages: both English and Bahasa Malaysia. At the time, AI was this new shiny thing that everyone seemed to talk about, so out of curiosity we experimented with it. Through that experience, we realized that the translations weren’t very natural-sounding and wouldn’t be faithful to the original text. So that’s when we stuck with our original plan, to work closely with a translator to do the translation itself. 

But then, as you mentioned, when it comes to publishing it is all about relationships and building connections. AI has been a great tool to draft emails when I’m reaching out to bookshops or retailers from around the world, like South America or Europe, where I don’t speak the language at all—like Spanish, for example. It does take a fair bit of prompting to get it right, but it is helpful to condense and convey to overseas retailers who we are and where we’re coming from as a small publisher in Malaysia. I think AI sort of helps with that. 

We were actually working with a bookshop in Seoul to stock our books there so we were doing a lot of email back and forth. When I finally met the retailer in person, she was actually very surprised that I didn’t speak Korean. She was like, “Oh my gosh, when you emailed me, I thought you spoke Korean natively because somehow you typed some good jokes in there.” I was so surprised by that as well. But then again, I can’t tell because I’m not a native speaker of Korean. So I guess in that sense, AI really helps in facilitating a lot of these human connections that are so important in this community. But in the actual editorial work—the stuff that will end up in the magazine—so far we find that perhaps the technology’s not quite there, or we just haven’t felt comfortable with it so far.

Sungil Noh

Yeah, I really agree with you because I started releasing my books abroad using AI translation. After using AI translation, I could reach bookstores and readers farther afield, so it was a very good opportunity for me. How about you, Wanda?

Wanda Kamarga

I have a similar experience to Kong Hui. During the early days of AI, we experimented with it a lot. At some book fairs abroad, we tried to make a small insert to explain the book. For example, there was one time we went to the Tokyo Art Book Fair. Because our book is in Bahasa Indonesia, we prepared a small insert, which was a translation of the whole book. But then, it didn’t sell. We thought maybe there was something wrong with how we did it, because we couldn’t read Japanese or Korean characters. One word can sometimes be one character, or sometimes three, and we didn’t know where to break the characters. Maybe something was wrong with that. So even with the help of AI, if we don’t understand the context, or if we copy and paste the words incorrectly, it doesn’t work.

So then we stopped, and we started using human translators to properly translate our books. Right now, we are translating one of our publications about football into Japanese, and we’re working closely with translators. They are really helpful because we have back-and-forth communication to check the cultural background—like “how to phrase this right” or “is this meaning wrong?” In general, AI bypasses this process of cultural exchange and understanding. When you try to do a cultural exchange without going through that process, it can cause misunderstandings.

Likewise, right now we are translating a work from Japanese to Bahasa Indonesia. Initially, the writer said, “I translated this quickly with AI so you understand the idea.” We read it, and then realized we had to work with human translators to do it right. So we figured that AI is very helpful as an assistant. If you want to understand things quickly or get your message across quickly to people in other languages, you do it with AI. But to execute a book well, it still needs real humans, because there’s a lot of process going on there.

Sungil Noh

Yeah, I feel the same as you. Sometimes I feel the barrier of language has been lowered with AI tools, so I can quickly contact others abroad. It was very insightful for me and gave me a lot of opportunities. It was very good.

Wanda Kamarga

So it helps make things faster, and it helps us simulate ideas faster when you don’t want to linger too long on an idea. But once you decide on it, you finish it up with real human work.

Sungil Noh

Yeah, I think this is a very easy tool for work, so sometimes I worry about losing my job. I want to ask you this: what are the biggest concerns among local writers and translators? Is it copyright, job replacement, or something like that?

Kong Hui

I can’t speak for all local authors and translators, but I think in the end AI will be here to stay, and the role of a human writer will change. As Wanda mentioned, oftentimes AI will provide you with the first draft of how the end product could potentially look, but that’s where skilled translators still come in and provide their perspective. In time, as AI becomes more commonplace, really good writers and authors could become even more important. Their work becomes even more apparent because everything else would sound or read the same due to AI. In a sense, AI will lift the floor of writing quality, but the ceiling also becomes even higher, so the good writers will shine more. On the ground, I think there is an understanding that AI is catching up, so it’s a challenge for everyone to develop their own perspective and style so we don’t end up doing something that AI can easily do. 

Wanda Kamarga

In Indonesia, the worry you mentioned about people getting laid off because of AI is already happening. Starting from this year, pretty much everyone has been talking about AI. But what’s been happening recently—and I hope it’s okay to share this—is that because I also run a design studio alongside publishing, I have two perspectives on this. People are jumping the gun on AI, thinking, “I can replace designers and creatives with this.” But they are starting to run into problems because they bypassed the creative process. When trouble happens and they have to troubleshoot, they don’t know how because they aren’t designers in the first place. So they come back to us saying, “We need your help. We need designers.” Fingers crossed, I hope this is a good sign, but that’s what’s happening.

In the world of creative communication, the biggest worry right now for a lot of Indonesian illustrators and artists is having their art fed into AI. This happens a lot, too. People even do witch-hunts, saying, “See? This is my art versus AI. I’m very sure somebody fed my art into AI.” So since last year, artists, writers, and creatives have been feeling very insecure about how their art is being fed into AI and used.

Sungil Noh

Yeah, that’s true. Many creators are feeling threatened by AI technology. We are going through a hard time and a revolutionary era. Let’s see how it unfolds in the future.

Wanda Kamarga

It’s pretty exciting, too, in a way.

Sungil Noh

Yeah. In this era, we need to talk more about AI tools and the usage of technology between the community and creators. Besides the questionnaire, I want to ask one more question: are there any cases or forums regarding AI adoption across different countries or in your own country?

Kong Hui

Yes, on a national level, there are some discussions. A lot of the discussions about AI by the government are very much focused on productivity—increasing GDP and all these metrics. On a creative, design, or art level, the general consensus is that it’s still not exactly the best for the community. As Wanda mentioned, it could be as bad as stealing original ideas or clients changing something without the designer’s knowledge. AI is still seen as not a good thing so far within the art and design community. But the government is trying to push it as a productivity tool that can improve people’s output.

Wanda Kamarga

Okay. For Indonesia, it’s pretty much a no. There’s no proper infrastructure—there’s really nothing yet. So especially for design and the creative sector, so far, there are almost no guardrails from the government.

Sungil Noh

In Korea, we have online communities. I think there are many kinds of AI clubs or communities where people want to learn more about new technology, because almost every worker uses AI tools these days for more efficient work. So if they hear news about new AI models, they go to online communities or blogs to learn about them. On a national level, I don’t think there’s much community-like activity, but our government wants to boost the AI industry more to compete with the US or China. So maybe in the future, on a national level, we will see some government-led communities or subsidies for it.

Wanda Kamarga

That is great, Sungil.

Realities of the Local Publishing Ecosystem & Perspectives on AI

Sungil Noh

Yeah, let’s go to the next question. I wonder about the burden of AI model subscription fees. Standard AI fees, like $20 per month for ChatGPT, can be heavy. Does this price barrier really stop publishers from adopting AI?

Kong Hui

For me, I don’t pay for any premium subscription so far. I use the free versions of these models, but you know, that’s because my usage is really quite light. A lot of my usage is just drafting emails or helping me to create an invoice, all these really little tasks. So thankfully, it doesn’t really use up so many of these tokens to the point where I need to use the premium version. But at the same time, I just feel like people here tend to be more resourceful. Let’s say, if you hit the limits on one service like ChatGPT, you could maybe switch to another service, like Gemini. If Gemini runs out, you switch to Claude. And if you run out again, you go somewhere else. Generally, the people I know who do pay for the premium version are people who are using it for their corporate day jobs. It’s a small sample size, so I am likely not painting the full picture here.

Wanda Kamarga

I think it’s similar in Indonesia. Most people probably still use the free version. I can’t speak for the whole nation because we are very diverse in terms of income and demographics, but I can speak for Jakarta. When it comes to individual use, I think most people just access the free version. But for professional use, $20 is still okay—that’s still affordable. Most studios or offices do subscribe.

Sungil Noh

In Korea, many people subscribe to the pro models of AI because they’re faster. You know, Korean people love to work faster and more efficiently.

Wanda Kamarga

Ppali-ppali (빨리빨리). Everyone.

Sungil Noh

Yeah, so many people subscribe to it. But generally, I think we don’t need to pay for pro models because we mostly do text-based work. So I think it’s okay in our industry, the publishing industry. However, as a designer, I use a pro subscription model because I need to generate images using credits. Text-based work and image-based work are quite different when it comes to subscriptions. So while many in the publishing industry use subscriptions, it is really expensive for me. As you know, OpenAI’s video model, Sora, is really expensive to use—the credits are so pricey that I can’t afford to use it every day.

Sungil Noh

Okay. Then I wonder about other publishers, because we are in a very niche market—like art books, or dealing with the art scene. But how about the usage of AI in the publishing industry in general, or in the broader market in your country, including commercial books or web novels? How is it?

Kong Hui

On the commercial side, I can’t really speak too much on their behalf, but online I definitely see AI being used—like for article summaries and quicker translations, especially by bigger news operations in Malaysia. At the same time, I don’t think they’re pushing it too hard for the end consumer just yet. It feels like they’re using it for smaller parts of their operations rather than actively promoting it. So that’s generally what I’ve seen so far.

Wanda Kamarga

Yeah. I don’t know much about the big commercial ones, but I think they’re not very dependent on writing with AI as such. Where I do see them using AI is in internet media—like social media accounts. Sometimes we can spot it and say, “Oh, this is written with AI.” Based on that, I presume that for longer reads that don’t require very short deadlines... if you have a longer timeline, they won’t switch to AI. They’ll say, “Oh, we’ll do it like humans normally do.” But with shorter formats and reads—for example, social media content and digital channels—you have to do it fast, right? Like, “Oh, this is today’s news. I have to launch it within an hour.” I’ve noticed they use AI to make the work quicker. So I think it has a lot to do with how much time is given.

Sungil Noh

Yeah, publishing always needs more time, but technology can reduce that time. It’s really helpful. I think it’s all relevant to the industry—not only the smaller sectors like independent publishers, but big ones as well. Both have opportunities.

Wanda Kamarga

Yes, but I’ve noticed that given the right amount of time, people still prefer doing it on their own. I see this starting to trend in Indonesia—this pride of saying, “I’m not using AI for this. This is purely my work.” So I think people still take pride in that. Given the choice and enough time, they will choose to do it manually.

Irreplaceable Values of Publishing & The Future of Asian Collaboration

Sungil Noh

Okay. What do you think is the most important part of publishing that AI can never replace?

Kong Hui

This is a question that I’m always thinking about a lot, especially since the early days of AI adoption. What differentiates something that was created by a large language model versus something that is created by a human being? Ultimately, if you average out the quality of writing across the board, it would be similar, but I think AI can never really replace the stories and the sort of experiences that a human being goes through. 

Oftentimes when I speak to our readers, I think that’s what they resonate the most with. No reader has told me, “Oh, I really like the grammatical arrangement of the sentences in the magazine,” or “I really like the way the words seem to have no typos.” People always say, “Oh, I really resonated with the story that writer wrote about because it was something that I went through as well. It was really comforting to see someone else going through that.” 

So I think for us, it’s really important to ensure that our editorial perspective remains unmoved. AI is helpful with the menial and time-consuming tasks like emails and invoicing. But I think the creative output itself has to always come from a sincere place, because our readers can tell when it does come from that place. That’s really something we feel that AI can never replace.

Wanda Kamarga

Yeah, I agree. It’s about sincerity and craftsmanship—especially when it comes to printed books, real tactile prints, and physical bindings that can never be replaced. So I’d say craftsmanship and penmanship. AI gives you predictability, but humans are wonderfully unpredictable. That will never be replaced by AI.

Sungil Noh

Yeah, I feel the exact same way. In the Korean publishing industry since the rise of AI, there has been a shift toward narrative-focused books like novels and essays. As Kong Hui said, AI cannot replace a good story, right? Readers want to imagine and connect through personal experiences, fiction, and essays, so the market for fiction and essays has grown significantly over the years.

Also, in Korea, independent book fairs are booming these days. This year was especially remarkable—I think more than thirty book fairs were organized nationwide. Local cities are eager to host their own book fairs because they are relatively easy to organize compared to large-scale festivals. In this era, physical craft and making things by hand have become even more special and irreplaceable. People want to touch and feel physical objects.

Kong Hui

You know what? I think over time you’ll start to see more and more people actually going back to all these analog things. We’ve seen this before. Like when cameras were all analog, and then we all went through the whole digital revolution, and everyone was like, “Oh, who’s going to use film anymore?” So then everyone switches to SD cards and pixels and all of that. But then we sort of realized over time, something is missing and we want to go back to the original feeling when you shoot something on analog film. And that’s probably what’s going to happen with books as well. People will realize that just reading something on a screen doesn’t hit the same as something they can touch, feel, and hold. So I think that’s probably playing out at the moment.

Wanda Kamarga

It’s kind of like a pendulum, right?

Sungil Noh

Yeah, exactly.

Wanda Kamarga

Last year, someone shared data with me showing that readership in Indonesia is actually rising. I can feel it firsthand because many bookstores stock our publications, and their reports reflect this. For instance, in Yogyakarta alone last month, several stores reported double the sales compared to previous periods. I think people are naturally trying to balance out the digital overload—partly caused by AI and technology—with something grounded, like physical books. 

Sungil Noh

“Like a pendulum,” right? That’s a great point. Okay, I have the final question for this session: what kind of solidarity and cooperation do we need to protect diversity and bring Asian publishers closer together?

Kong Hui

Well, a conversation like this, I think that’s always good, having the opportunity to meet publishers like Wanda. I’ve been following Binatang Press for a long, long time. I have a few titles at home, you know, like the fried chicken zine. 

Wanda Kamarga

Thank you.

Kong Hui

I think a lot of these exchanges are good because everyone is going through a version of something similar. Events like Art Book Fairs across the region have also really taken off as well, which I find very helpful. Like, I have friends and publishers from Indonesia, like Daud from Petrikor Books. It’s always nice to speak to him, and you just realize how similar everyone ultimately is. I think it’s really great to get these opportunities to speak to one another.

Wanda Kamarga

I agree 100%. Doing these kinds of conversations and exchanges naturally leads to ideas like, “Oh, we should host more of these here,” or “Let’s organize another one there.” 

Sungil Noh

That’s so true. I’m really happy to meet both of you today. Having known each other through book fairs over the past four years, I genuinely feel like you are my friends and colleagues in this industry. Meeting creators and publishers at book fairs feels like an annual family reunion. It brings us together and makes us stronger, right?

Wanda Kamarga

In my studio, whenever a book fair season ends, everyone always says, “Oh, I already miss the book fair! Where is the next one?”

Kong Hui

It’s always so fun. I think just meeting friends and generally hanging out, having a lot of food, I think it’s always nice. It’s like changing the scenery each time. It’s always fun.

Sungil Noh

Yeah. So that is our good weapon against new technology or with new technology, so we can see the future together, right? 

Wanda Kamarga

At Binatang Press, it’s not like we’re against AI. It’s very useful, but the lesson after two years of experimenting with AI is how you choose your weapon—or, how should I put it, you cannot use this for everything. Choose wisely in which area you want to utilize AI. In our case, we use it a lot to process data like sales reports and inventory. You know, the things that we creators are actually lazy about doing, we give that to AI.

Sungil Noh

Right, it’s not a weapon, but a tool—a utility.

Wanda Kamarga

Exactly. Choosing the right tool for the right job.

Kong Hui

As independent publishers and magazine makers, ultimately we are just small businesses, right? In the sense that resources are tight. So I resonate with what Wanda mentioned, because AI really helps to free up and save a lot of time from menial tasks that eventually goes back into creative work. Because I’m always trying to see how I can find more time for that. So AI is a great tool to help us save time to put into what matters.

Sungil Noh

Thank you so much for your time and insights today.

Kong Hui

Thanks for having us!

Wanda Kamarga

Thank you so much, guys. This was really fun!

About the Contributors

Sungil Noh Graphic designer and publisher. He runs Sojanggak, a publishing house and design studio in Seoul, and works across Asia’s art book fairs.

Kong Hui Founder and editor of Process Magazine, a Kuala Lumpur-based publication documenting creative practices across Malaysia and Southeast Asia.

Wanda Kamarga Creative director at the Jakarta design studio The 1984 and the independent publisher Binatang Press; a member of YPSI, which runs the Press Print Party book fair.
