Q&ATaiwan

Taiwan Has No AI Copyright Rules Yet. Publishers Can’t Wait for Them.

Drawing on recent cases in Taiwan where copyright law, court rulings and policy are making legal risks concrete, the author outlines the legal safeguards publishers need to put in place for the age of AI.

Chun-Wei Tseng Attorney, Taiwan

Question 1. How is AI training data currently treated under Taiwan’s copyright law?

Taiwan has not yet enacted copyright rules specifically governing “AI training data,” and no court has issued a ruling directly determining whether the use of AI training data is lawful. At this stage, therefore, the legal status of AI training data must be assessed under Taiwan’s existing Copyright Act.

1. AI training may reproduce source materials and potentially infringe the copyright owner’s reproduction right

Taiwan’s Intellectual Property Office stated in an August 29, 2025, interpretation that activities undertaken during AI training—including data collection, preprocessing, model training and optimization—may involve the “reproduction” of source materials and therefore may potentially infringe a copyright owner’s reproduction right.

2. AI-generated outputs may infringe the copyright owner’s right of adaptation

In the same August 29, 2025, interpretation, the Intellectual Property Office explained that where AI makes no separate creative contribution to an original work, the process does not constitute an “adaptation” and therefore does not, on that basis, raise an infringement issue involving the copyright in the original training data. Conversely, if works contained in a training database are “collaged” or “recombined” and the resulting output is substantially similar to the original training work, the output may infringe the copyright owner’s right of adaptation.

3. Copyright protection for AI-generated output depends on sufficient human creative contribution

With respect to AI-generated content, the Intellectual Property Office stated in interpretations issued on June 11, 2018 and April 1, 2025 that purely AI-generated works with no human creative input are not protected by copyright. Where a human makes an actual creative contribution and AI is used merely as an assisting tool, however, the resulting work may still qualify for copyright protection.

Question 2. Have there been significant court decisions or legislative changes in Taiwan?

1. Significant court decision

Taiwan has not yet produced a court ruling directly addressing the legality of AI training data. There has, however, been a case involving the use of web crawlers to copy a legal database in which the court indicated that the fact that data were acquired “to train AI and enable AI to learn” cannot, by itself, serve as a blanket defense. Taiwanese courts have also held that where reproduction of another party’s work negatively affects that party’s market, the reproduction may fail the fair-use test and constitute copyright infringement.

New Taipei District Court ruling

In New Taipei District Court Judgment No. 111-Zhi-Su-8, issued June 24, 2025, and currently under appeal, Qifa Co., Ltd. (operator of the “Lawsnote” legal database service) and two founders were prosecuted for using web-crawling software to copy and download 98,068 records of legislative histories from another legal database, place them in their own database, and monetize access through monthly membership fees. The court found that the conduct constituted a copyright offense involving unauthorized reproduction for the purpose of sale. The two founders were sentenced to four years and two years’ imprisonment, respectively; approximately NT$4.625 million and NT$3.7 million in criminal proceeds were confiscated, and the legal database company was fined NT$1.5 million.

Reference to a U.S. case

The district court further cited Thomson Reuters v. Ross Intelligence in the United States, a case involving extensive copying of legal database materials to train an in-house AI-powered legal research system. The court noted that the defendant’s product could substitute for the complainant’s product in the market and could affect the potential market for licensing the complainant’s data as AI training material. On that basis, it concluded that the defendant did not satisfy the requirements for fair use. The decision also emphasized that using data “to train AI so that AI can learn” is not, as a general rule, a blanket exemption from liability.

2. Legislative developments

As of now, Taiwan has not enacted dedicated copyright rules for AI training data. A potentially important policy development is the Artificial Intelligence Basic Act, promulgated and brought into force on January 14, 2026. Article 13 requires the government to improve the quality and quantity of AI data while protecting intellectual property rights. Article 18 requires the competent authorities to review and adjust relevant laws and administrative measures within two years. More specific copyright rules concerning AI training data could therefore emerge and take effect within that period.

Question 3. What legal measures is Taiwan’s publishing industry currently taking?

Taiwan’s publishing industry does not yet have a unified AI-use policy or a collective licensing system for copyrighted works. Individual publishers and media organizations are nevertheless taking several measures.

1. Publicly prohibiting AI use

Some media organizations have begun expressly prohibiting users, through membership terms or copyright notices, from providing articles, images, audio, video, or database content to generative AI systems for training, fine-tuning, generation, or derivative uses. For example, the membership terms of Commonwealth Magazine Group include restrictions of this kind. They prohibit members, without the group’s express written authorization, from inputting, uploading, integrating, or otherwise providing the group’s content to generative AI systems, platforms, or models for training, fine-tuning, generation, reuse, or other derivative purposes. Where cooperation or licensing is required, members are instructed to contact the group in advance to obtain appropriate authorization and guidance. The terms add that respecting intellectual property is a civic duty, and that any member who violates the clause shall be liable to Commonwealth Magazine Group for damages, including but not limited to litigation costs and attorneys’ fees.

2. Establishing internal AI-use policies

Some media organizations have also adopted internal AI-use policies. On July 17, 2023, the head of content at Commonwealth Magazine Group set out AI-use guidelines requiring all published content to undergo human review, editing, and fact-checking, while prohibiting the direct use of AI-generated articles, images, and videos. The organization has also emphasized transparency by disclosing AI-related applications used by its editorial operation and continuing to work with credible organizations so that AI serves as a tool for media professionals rather than a source of fake news or misinformation.

3. Self-regulation at the creation stage

Major Taiwanese literary competitions, including the Lin Rong-san Literary Award, Taipei Literary Award, and the Taiwan Mystery Writers’ Association writing competition, strictly prohibit AI ghostwriting. Sanctions may include disqualification, recovery of prize money and trophies, public disclosure of the violation, and lifetime bans from participating in the competitions.

Question 4. What should the publishing industry be preparing for now as it enters the AI era?

1. Establish internal AI-use guidelines

A publisher faces two risks if it opposes unauthorized AI use of its own content while simultaneously allowing editors to paste manuscripts into public generative AI tools. First, the manuscript may be exposed or leaked. Second, AI-generated material may be incorporated into a publication, creating uncertainty over whether the publication qualifies for copyright protection and potentially resulting in infringement of third-party copyrights. The publisher may bear responsibility for these risks.

Strict internal guidelines—such as requiring human review of all content and prohibiting the direct use of AI-generated material—can materially reduce these risks. Publishers should also address whether authors used AI in their submission agreements, potentially requiring authors to sign a “declaration of non-use of AI.” Strong internal controls will provide a firmer basis for asserting rights externally in the future.

2. Even where the law is silent, AI-training provisions must be included in notices and contracts

Taiwan’s Copyright Act does not currently expressly determine whether AI training constitutes infringement. As a result, copyright notices and contracts are the only tools publishers can control themselves.

Externally, publishers should expressly prohibit AI training in membership terms, copyright notices, and copyright pages. A clause like the one in Commonwealth Magazine Group’s membership terms, prohibiting users from providing content to generative AI for training, fine-tuning, generation, or derivative purposes, can serve as evidence that the copyright owner did not implicitly consent to AI training. It may also preserve a basis for arguing that a future infringement was willful and for negotiating a license.

Internally, new publishing agreements should expressly address whether AI training, fine-tuning, retrieval, and related uses fall within the licensed rights, how revenue will be allocated, and whether authors retain an opt-out right. Under Article 37 of Taiwan’s Copyright Act, where the scope of a license is unclear, the principle is that the use is presumed not to have been authorized. In other words, if the contract does not address an AI-related use, the publisher may not possess that right. Failure to address the issue proactively could later call into question the publisher’s authority to negotiate AI-training licenses on behalf of authors.

3. The Readmoo incident: prevent data theft and prepare for future infringement litigation

On August 8, 2026, Taiwan’s leading local e-book platform Readmoo (讀墨) suffered a large-scale, high-intensity malicious-traffic and hacker attack. Although the platform’s core asset—the digital files of e-books—was not breached or stolen, the incident nevertheless disrupted the service for several days.

In the AI era, publishers must strengthen access controls, encryption, and backup systems for copyrighted files. No matter how comprehensive their contracts and notices may be, once large quantities of content are stolen and incorporated into someone else’s training dataset, it becomes extremely difficult to recover the material afterward.

Prevention, however, is only half the task. If a publisher later seeks to establish infringement, it must be able to produce evidence showing who stole what content and when. Publishers should therefore establish procedures at an early stage for identifying, documenting, and preserving evidence of data theft. Without preserved evidence, even stringent legal rules and carefully drafted notices and contracts may provide little practical leverage in asserting rights.

4. Establish a collective copyright licensing system

A “collective licensing system” would pool works from multiple rights holders and allow a representative organization to negotiate with AI training organizations on a unified basis, collect licensing fees, and distribute the proceeds to the individual rights holders. Such a system would enable smaller rights holders to receive compensation as well.

Taiwan currently has no collective licensing gateway specifically for AI training, and licensing depends largely on individual negotiations. The National Science and Technology Council’s TAIDE project is a representative publicly disclosed example of paid licensing in Taiwan. Through the National Applied Research Laboratories’ Center for Science and Technology Policy, the project negotiated individually with content organizations and ultimately reached agreements with the Central News Agency (30 years of news, 1993–2023), Business Today (articles from 2008–2023), ETtoday, and Taiwan Panorama (光華雜誌), among others. Each organization received several million New Taiwan dollars in licensing fees.

The example illustrates the limitation created by the absence of a collective licensing system: only large organizations with substantial volumes of content and concentrated rights are well positioned to negotiate AI-training transactions, while small publishers and individual authors may be excluded from the market. The lack of a collective licensing mechanism can therefore also make it harder for AI developers to secure sufficient high-quality training data.

About the Contributors

Chun-Wei Tseng Copyright attorney in Taiwan.

InterviewJapan

AI Is a Tool. The Power of Story Remains Human.

Toshihiro Sato, who leads AI and data strategy at Kodansha, one of Japan’s largest publishers, explains what the company is building, what it means to protect, and why editors stand to gain.

Toshihiro Sato Director, AI & Data Strategy Department, Kodansha

Self-Introduction and the Role of Kodansha’s AI & Data Strategy Department

My name is Toshihiro Sato, and I work in the AI & Data Strategy Department of Kodansha’s IT Strategy Planning Division. After working as a project manager and in other roles in the anime and gaming industries, I joined Kodansha in 2012. I have worked on a range of projects, including developing internal systems and providing hands-on support to business units. I have held my current position since 2026.

The IT Strategy Planning Division is responsible for business development based on digital technology, collaboration with outside companies, the operation and management of internal systems, and infrastructure development.

Within the division, the AI & Data Strategy Department leads efforts to build data infrastructure and develop strategies and governance for the use of AI and data at Kodansha and its group companies.

Specific Examples of AI Use in Publishing

Our work includes AI development projects and sharing information about generative AI.

Development Diary: The RD Nurturing Project

Our department also develops Kodansha’s own AI products. The RD Nurturing Project began with the challenge of exploring whether AI could recreate a character, while we were considering a business collaboration with Tohoku University in Japan. Developed using natural language processing (NLP), it is a project to nurture RD, an artificial intelligence character from the Kaito Queen (Phantom Thief Queen) series, together with fans. We have also received very positive reactions from fans who feel passionately about the character, and the results have exceeded our expectations.

Supporting and Governing AI Use In-House

We also work to raise awareness within the company of AI-related technologies such as those mentioned above.

We have also established a task force that brings together staff from relevant departments to respond to AI-related inquiries and assess the risks of internal AI use. Inquiries come in every day without letup from business, administrative, sales, and other departments, and I feel there is tremendous enthusiasm for using AI within the company.

At the same time, AI services are evolving so quickly that we find it challenging to adapt our internal governance and rules flexibly in response. We have come to realize that introducing AI tools alone is not enough: how thoroughly workflows have been organized beforehand is an extremely important prerequisite.

The Convergence of Roles in AI and Publishing: Future Outlook

No one knows what the future holds, but I feel that, at present, generative AI is by no means producing works that move people in a fundamental way. The ability to create stories that stir readers’ emotions and change their outlook on life remains a uniquely human domain. Genuine achievements by AI in this area are likely still a long way off.

That is why, at a time of rapid technological progress, those of us in publishing need to consider how to engage with AI as a powerful tool and support human creativity, rather than simply whether to let AI create works. There are two sides to this: areas we must protect without compromise, and areas we must boldly seek to transform as times change.

1. Areas to Protect: Creators’ Rights and a Broad View of Risk

Our first priority must be to protect authors’ and creators’ rights and a healthy environment for their creative work. We need to keep pace with questions of legal interpretation, including the flexible copyright exceptions under Article 30-4 of Japan’s Copyright Act for uses not intended for the enjoyment of a work’s expressed thoughts or feelings, as well as the rapid evolution of AI technology, and share what we learn with creators.

It is particularly important to recognize that creators have very different views, feelings, and positions on AI. Some are eager to use it, while others naturally feel anxious or resistant. We urgently need research into how AI can be used safely and effectively in creative work while respecting these diverse views and preserving authors’ rights.

As works are increasingly distributed overseas, we must also pay close attention to differences in audience reactions across countries and regions. Alongside appropriate consideration of national laws, including the EU AI Act, we need to address regional ethical perspectives and cultural reputational risks. Maximizing authors’ rights and interests requires a highly nuanced sense of balance in deciding where to use AI and where to deliberately refrain from using it.

2. Areas to Transform: Digital Transformation and “Agentification” of Publishing Workflows

On the other hand, we need to make bold changes to reduce the workload borne by authors, creators, and their editors. In essence, this means fundamentally transforming publishing workflows through digital technology. Publishing’s long history also means that established practices and labor-intensive manual tasks have often become routine. The key is to establish clear guardrails for acceptable risk while determining how to achieve the “agentification” of these tasks with AI—that is, using AI agents to automate or assist with them. Setting priorities and developing guidelines in this previously uncharted area of AI is an urgent task. The change we seek is an environment in which editors and creators can devote their passion to distinctly human creative work, such as developing new ideas and making a work as compelling as possible, rather than being overwhelmed by administrative tasks.

3. New Experiences and the Evolution of Development Processes

We have also begun researching ways to create new user experiences beyond improvements in operational efficiency. AI-powered conversational bot services, for example, offer fans a richer experience by allowing them to interact with characters rather than simply read the works. We are also beginning to use data and AI, including predictions of a work’s success and assessments of its value, to reach new readers and customers whom we have not reached before, rather than relying solely on past experience. Major changes are also taking place in development. Faster coding with AI has substantially reduced development costs and dramatically shortened the cycle from an idea to a prototype. In response, we would also like to adapt and evolve our existing product management and development operations frameworks to make them more flexible and responsive.

In Closing

No matter how far technology advances, human passion and the joy of creation remain at the heart of a work. By using AI properly and skillfully, we can firmly protect creators’ rights while renewing established systems that need to change, and bring works and readers together around the world. I feel that keeping both of these efforts moving forward is our mission in this era.

In-Depth Follow-Up Questions and Answers

Question 1. When considering potential risks associated with internal AI use, which assessment criteria do you prioritize most highly?

We place the greatest importance on two aspects: legal and technical considerations. On the legal side, we closely monitor the latest case law and the implementation of laws in each country, and rigorously assess the effects on copyright holders’ rights and the publishing industry. On the technical side, we assess technical stability and security risks, focusing on major updates to leading LLMs and similar developments.

Question 2. As you move toward the “agentification” of publishing workflows with AI, could you share one specific task or framework that you are currently prioritizing for practical application?

The fundamental prerequisite is to establish strong governance covering the prevention of internal data leaks, information security, and copyright clearance. We, too, are only now reaching the stage of beginning full-scale work on designing specific assessment criteria and operating rules.

Building on that strong governance, our highest priority for workflow digital transformation is an “Expanded Search System for Published Works.” In a publishing business that handles a wide range of titles, well-timed and precisely targeted sales initiatives directly affect revenue. With so many works entrusted to us every day, we want to use AI to improve the accuracy of information about their release dates, core themes, and detailed target audiences from multiple angles, so that they reach readers rather than becoming buried in the market.

For example, adding accurate metadata about works to semantic search systems or the knowledge bases searched by AI agents can fundamentally prevent appealing books from becoming buried in a vast catalog and enable us to reach the readers they should reach.

At the same time, editors will be freed from administrative tasks such as organizing data and entering attributes, allowing them to concentrate on developing substantive sales strategies. We also expect significant benefits for creators, as their works gain exposure in the most suitable form and their sales opportunities are maximized.

Note: These are my personal views and do not represent the views of Kodansha.

EssayIndonesia

In Indonesia, Nearly Everyone Can Read. Far Fewer Read Books.

Literacy has never been higher across the archipelago, yet the reading habit lags. An Indonesian publisher on how AI is reshaping what people read, and who should shape what comes next.

Aniesah Hasan Syihab Director and Co-founder, BACA Publishing House

Indonesia has a complicated relationship with reading. With a population of roughly 284 million spread across more than 17,000 islands, reading habits here have never been uniform, and they are shifting again as artificial intelligence continues to rise. As someone who has spent the past decade running a book publishing house in the country, I have watched this shift unfold not as an abstract trend but as something that shapes what we publish, how we sell, and how our readers talk to us every day.

Where reading culture stands today

Indonesia’s National Statistics Agency, Badan Pusat Statistik (BPS), recorded an adult literacy rate of 97.1 percent in 2025, the highest in a decade. The figure refers to the proportion of Indonesians aged 15 and over who are able to read and write a simple sentence. Yet the ability to read and the habit of reading books are two different things, as Indonesia’s scores in the OECD’s PISA reading assessment have declined over the past three cycles, and reading-frequency surveys from BPS have long shown that regular book reading remains a minority habit compared to the country’s near-universal literacy.

What has grown enormously is the amount of time Indonesians spend reading in other forms. Indonesia had about 212 million internet users at the start of 2025, about 75 percent of the population, and later data from the Indonesian Internet Service Providers Association (APJII) put that closer to 81 percent by year’s end. This expansion of connectivity has also widened access to digital reading: for millions of Indonesians, books, articles, news, and other written content are now potentially available online regardless of where they live. At the same time, with 143 million people active on social media, a huge amount of daily reading now happens in WhatsApp threads, Instagram captions, news headlines, and serialized fiction on local apps.

Physical bookstores remain concentrated in Jakarta and a handful of other major cities, while access elsewhere depends heavily on school libraries, secondhand markets, and increasingly, online marketplaces and delivery. One thing that has genuinely surprised me is how much physical reading spaces have come back, just in a different shape. The rise of aesthetic, Instagram-friendly bookstores and book cafes, particularly around Yogyakarta and Jakarta, are increasingly designed as attractive social spaces, combining books with coffee, art, design, and community. I went to ten of these bookstores in Yogyakarta myself, and the pattern was obvious: people come first for the space, and the books follow. Some of these places have gone properly viral. Whether that turns into people actually reading more, or just visiting more, is a fair question, but at minimum it is putting books back in front of people who might otherwise never walk into a bookstore.

Format and language also tell a layered story. Indonesian-language books dominate general readership, but English-language titles in self-improvement, business, and popular fiction carry strong prestige among younger, urban, educated readers, while translated foreign literature has become a genuine growth category over the past several years. Print remains dominant, but audio is a newer and increasingly visible entry point. Storytel, the Swedish audiobook and e-book subscription service, launched in Indonesia in 2022 with more than 150,000 audiobook and e-book titles in Indonesian, English, and Mandarin. Its local catalog has included works by prominent Indonesian authors, with well-known actors and authors such as Dian Sastrowardoyo, Fedi Nuril, Chicco Jerikho, and Dewi Lestari lending their voices to selected titles. The format offers another way into books, particularly for commuters and people who find it difficult to sit down with a physical book, allowing stories to fit more easily into everyday routines.

What ties all of this together is that reading in Indonesia is becoming more social and shaped by how people discover books. People often encounter books online before seeing them in a bookstore, through social media, recommendations, digital platforms, or short-form content. These discoveries can turn reading into something people share, discuss, and recommend, shaping not only what they read but how they engage with books.

How AI is reshaping discovery and access

Recommendation systems on platforms such as TikTok, Instagram, YouTube, and online bookstores have become an increasingly important layer between readers and books. The rise of BookTok and Bookstagram is one visible example. In Indonesia, book creators and literary communities use short-form video to recommend and review books, while publishers and booksellers increasingly respond to what gains traction online. Windy Ariestanty, founder of the Patjarmerah Literary Festival, said in 2025 that the growth of book content on TikTok had coincided with increased book purchases and the emergence of alternative bookstores, with some retailers creating dedicated shelves for books that go viral. Algorithms do not just recommend more books; they can put a book in front of someone who was never looking for it, and turn a private reading choice into something shared and talked about.

But discovery does not only happen to readers through their feeds anymore. I do not do this often, but when I have a specific, hard-to-place question, I have asked an AI tool for book recommendations myself, once for a list of classic Middle Eastern literature I was struggling to track down through the usual channels. That is a different kind of discovery than an algorithm deciding what to show me. Someone looking for books on a particular subject can ask an AI tool to suggest titles, compare them, explain what each is about, and narrow down what is actually worth reading. The recommendations still need to be checked: AI can misunderstand a request, miss important titles, or simply get things wrong, but it shortens the distance between “I want to learn about this” and having an actual list of books to start with.

Translation is where AI’s role in publishing needs to be described most carefully. In publishing, it can help editors assess foreign-language manuscripts, compare passages, check terminology, identify obvious errors, and work more quickly through large amounts of text during the early stages of acquisition and editing. It can therefore lower some of the time and cost involved in evaluating foreign titles. But for publication itself, the translation still depends on professional human translators, whose work involves voice, tone, cultural context, rhythm, and interpretation.

AI is also beginning to make text more accessible in different formats. Text-to-speech and AI-assisted voice technologies can turn written material into audio, while audiobook platforms offer another way of fitting books into everyday routines, during commutes, household tasks, or other moments when sitting down with a physical book is not possible. The significance may be less that Indonesians are abandoning print than that the boundaries of what counts as reading are becoming more flexible. A person can encounter a book through a TikTok recommendation, ask an AI tool for similar titles, read a sample on a phone, listen to part of it while traveling, and then buy a physical copy.

The most positive change may simply be that AI makes discovering and choosing books easier and more personalized. Social platforms can then turn those discoveries into shared conversations and communities. AI does not automatically create readers, but it can make the journey from curiosity to a book easier, and increasingly, more social.

The risks beneath the growth

The concerns are just as real as the opportunities. One of the most immediate risks is the sheer volume of AI-generated and algorithmically curated content competing for the same attention that reading once occupied. There is a legitimate concern that habits formed around short-form video and constantly changing feeds may make sustained attention—the kind required by a novel, a long-form essay, or a serious work of nonfiction—feel increasingly difficult, particularly for younger readers who are growing up inside these platforms. Indonesian researchers studying BookTok itself have noted this tension: the same algorithmic curation that can revive interest in reading also rewards content built around strong emotional reactions and social validation rather than critical engagement. A book can become highly visible because it is trending, but visibility does not necessarily translate into deeper or more critical reading.

Another concern comes from the growing popularity of book-summary platforms and AI-generated summaries. Apps such as Blinkist and Headway, which have each attracted tens of millions of users globally by promising busy readers the “key ideas” of a book in fifteen minutes, have found an audience in Indonesia too, alongside local and regional entrants such as Pimtar and the Singapore-based NexPage, both of which market themselves explicitly to Indonesian-language readers. Their appeal is easy to understand: I was once targeted by one of these platforms’ marketing myself, subscribed, and genuinely enjoyed several of the summaries. Used selectively, this can be a real gateway into a book, not a substitute for it. But over time, I found I preferred returning to the physical book itself, and eventually unsubscribed. The risk is that fewer readers make that same return trip. If readers become accustomed to consuming only the key points, they may gradually lose the patience or motivation required for sustained reading. What disappears in the process is not simply detail. Full books contain context, nuance, evidence, narrative development, ambiguity, and the connections between ideas that a summary necessarily leaves out. A reader may come away knowing what a book says without having experienced how the author arrived there, or why the argument, story, or ideas matter.

The rise of AI-generated books makes the role of the reader more important, not less. Some publishing services in Indonesia are already experimenting with AI to generate book content, and some openly acknowledge AI’s role in the production process. This makes it increasingly important for readers to know what they are choosing to read and to distinguish between books shaped primarily by humans and those generated by machines. To be clear, AI can be genuinely skillful. It can produce fluent, coherent, and highly polished prose, and at times it can even move a reader, in the moment. But I do not think it can consistently do what human writing does at its best. Readers can usually feel the difference when a book carries something a machine cannot manufacture: a voice shaped by lived experience, years of study, emotions, cultural specificity, and the imperfections that make a story feel genuinely human. It shows most clearly in the rare books that stay with you, that move you, or make you cry, the ones written by someone who had something deeply personal to say. AI may make it easier and cheaper to produce books, but it does not necessarily make those books more meaningful. Readers will need to exercise their own judgment about which books deserve their attention, money, and appreciation.

The access divide may be the most structurally important concern. The people most likely to benefit from AI-enhanced reading tools are those who already have reliable internet access, suitable devices, digital literacy, and the confidence to evaluate and verify what AI produces. These advantages are unevenly distributed across Indonesia. The digital divide is therefore not simply about who is online and who is offline; it is also about the quality of access and the skills needed to turn connectivity into meaningful use. Without deliberate effort, AI could end up reinforcing the existing divide between people who already have abundant access to books, information, and cultural resources and those who have much less. The risk is that AI makes the reading-rich even more efficient at finding and consuming knowledge, while doing less to reach the people who are already furthest from books and reading opportunities.

What Indonesia’s reading culture needs next

The use of AI in reading and literacy is not really up for debate anymore. It is already happening, it cannot realistically be stopped, and treating it as optional would be a mistake. The real question is not whether AI belongs in Indonesia’s reading culture, but how deliberately the country shapes that role. Publishers have a part to play in setting quality and transparency standards, including clear disclosure when AI has been used in translation, summary, or content generation, so readers can trust what they are engaging with. Industry associations could usefully establish shared guidelines here before the market fills that vacuum with lower-quality, unregulated AI content, a pattern already visible in more mature markets.

Ikapi (Ikatan Penerbit Indonesia), the country’s publishers’ association, has yet to issue formal guidelines on how AI can be used in writing or publishing books. Its own chairman, Arys Hilman Nugraha, acknowledged this gap in a July 2026 interview, noting that Malaysia and Singapore have already begun drafting AI regulations for their publishing industries while Indonesia’s attention remains focused on unresolved book piracy. Ikapi is well positioned to set that standard, covering questions like how much AI involvement should be disclosed and where AI-assisted work ends and AI-generated work begins, before the market sets it by default.

Government and educational institutions have a complementary role in strengthening digital and information literacy alongside traditional literacy programs. Indonesia’s Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education made this connection explicit at last year’s International Literacy Day, choosing “Kesalehan Literasi Digital, Membangun Peradaban” (roughly, “Virtuous Digital Literacy, Building Civilization”) as the national theme, treating the ability to evaluate a source or a recommendation algorithm as seriously as the ability to read a sentence. Continued infrastructure investment, particularly internet access and device affordability outside Java, remains the precondition for any AI-enabled reading benefit to reach the regions that need it most.

Civil society and community reading initiatives, meanwhile, are where I remain most optimistic. Independent bookstores, reading communities, and grassroots literacy programs across Indonesia have consistently shown an ability to make reading feel communal and aspirational in ways no algorithm can replicate on its own. The most promising path forward pairs AI’s genuine strengths in access and discovery with the human, community-driven infrastructure that has always been the real engine of reading culture in Indonesia. The technology can widen the door. It is still up to publishers, educators, and readers themselves to make sure people want to walk through it.

About the Contributors

Aniesah Hasan Syihab Director and co-founder of BACA Publishing House in Indonesia and, by her own description, a professional tsundoku: someone who buys books faster than she can read them.
